Discover Board Game Arena Rules summary The inhabitants of the villages surrounding a dormant volcano were happily living in peace until — KABOOM! — the old volcano sprang back to life, unleashing rivers of molten lava in every direction and blasting volcanic rock into the sky. The villages, now faced with destruction, must do whatever they can to protect their homes from the incoming surge of lava. Your village is about to burn up — can you take the heat? Contents 1 Overview 2 Turns 3 Burn Meter 4 Ending the Game Overview Players control villages that are threatened by an erupting volcano. Protect your village by placing lava tiles and building walls strategically, while also trying to direct lava toward the other villages to gain valuable action cards. The player whose village is at the lowest temperature at the end of the game, wins. Turns Do the following on each turn, in order: 1) Assess damage - your village heats up 20 degrees on the Burn Meter for each lava flow entering your village that is not blocked by a wall. For each lava flow that is blocked by a wall, roll the dice; if the lava (orange) wins the roll, your village heats up 10 degrees and the wall is discarded. If the wall is wood, add 1 point to the white die; if the wall is stone, add 2 points to the white die. Lava (orange) wins ties. 2) Draw and place a lava tile - place the tile so that all lava flows and grassy areas connect properly to other tiles. If you place a tile on a resource space, you gain a wall of that material. After placing a tile next to a village, a player may draw one (1) Action Card for each new lava flow in contact with the village. ( Note : 1 card per lava flow , not 1 per lava tile , so this can be one or two cards, depending). If you want to place a tile next to a lava flow that is blocked with a wall, you must roll the dice and the lava must win the dice roll (or else you have to place the tile elsewhere). 3) Play as many action cards as desired - you can only keep a maximum of 3 Action Cards at the end of your turn. To play a card, discard it and either carry out the effect shown on the card or retrieve a wall of the material shown (you cannot do both). You can also optionally discard 2 cards to gain an additional tile placement. Aftershock (×5) Wall Equivalent: Stone - Allows a player to rotate any tile on the board to any position. The tile must remain in its current location. No tiles may violate standard tile placement rules due to the rotation of the tile. Any walls on the tile are immediately discarded. Lava Flow (×3) Wall Equivalent: Straw - Allows a player to draw and place a new Lava Tile following standard tile placement rules. Relocate (×5) Wall Equivalent: Straw - Allows a player to move one or more walls in their village to any other location within the village. After doing so, no more than one wall may exist in any location. Sinkhole (×4) Wall Equivalent: Wood - Allows a player to discard any existing tile from the board, along with any walls built on it. No tiles may violate standard tile placement rules due to the removal of the tile. Quake (×5) Wall Equivalent: Stone - Allows a player to draw a new Lava Tile and immediately replace any existing tile on the board. The new tile must follow standard tile placement rules. The old tile, along with any walls built on it, is discarded from the board. If no replacements can be made, the tile is placed randomly within the stack and another tile is drawn. If the new tile creates new connections to a village, draw one (1) Action card for each new lava flow in contact with the village. Rain (×4) Wall Equivalent: Wood - Allows a player to immediately cool down their own village by 30 degrees on the Burn Meter. Reinforce (×6) Wall Equivalent: Straw - Allows a player to immediately build a wall from their stockpile, in addition to the one wall normally allowed at the end of the turn. community_text:
[Rating: 1/10] Not to my taste. Superficially looks like a family game but has some issues: – Catch up mechanic is overly beneficial so losing early is a good way to win – Playtime of 50 mins is too long for what this game offers – Rain cards are great near the end, so swingy – Tile draws are random, some amazing, some ok

[Rating: 1.5/10] Worse than most random, "take that" games because several rules and mechanics seem to be very unbalanced.

[Rating: 2/10] Once I was hit i just continued to get burned.  With absolutely no way I could win.  Not that I didn't cause some havoc for those that attacked me, but there was no catching up. I'm ok with a king making style game but this one was over the top.

[Rating: 2/10] Interesting idea but it is far too easy for players to gang up on someone with no recourse. I would play it as a team endeavor, but not as a free-for-all.

[Rating: 2/10] This game is broken in that pouring lava onto your own village is a very good strategy because of the incredibly powerful bonuses you will receive. Doesn't make sense IMO

[Rating: 2/10] Weirdly strategic tile placement. Decent, but can't get behind the strategy idea. Requires early sacrifice to get more tiles. With more players also more random.

[Rating: 2.5/10] Played on BGA, and it is just bad. Very much attack others to try and burn down their villages. Luck of the draw for cards and tiles. All around, just not fun and not a game I would care to ever play again.

[Rating: 3/10] Eruption has some serious problems. The game is quite slow for a light take-that game. Losing early seems overly beneficial as the  catch-up mechanism seems out of balance, giving the game a (seemingly) unintended lose-to-win feel. The cards don't feel particularly balanced either, as players who can stock pile rain cards can make huge scoring swings on their last turn without risk of retaliation. And, lastly turn order seems to have an excessively large influence on determining the victor. If volcanoes are your thing, The Downfall of Pompeii is a substantially superior game.

[Rating: 3/10] This game feels like something published in the 80s, that you would find under your Christmas tree along with a box of pralines, back when board games were associated with Monopoly and UNO only. Quick gameplay, not requiring much strategy... just your standard 80s board game.
